title: forest loss accelerates can world meet rising demand wood  ecmii 2026 09 09
text:
September 9 - With the impacts of climate change being felt across the globe, forests are under pressure as never before.
While agriculture is the main driver of permanent deforestation, wildfires contributed 30% of tree cover loss and logging accounted for a 25% loss between 2001 and 2025, according to WRI.
This loss may be temporary, but forests can take decades to recover and may never return to full health. Boreal forests have been ravaged to make toilet paper, while in Europe wood pellets are burned for energy.
Five years after countries pledged to halt and reverse forest loss by 2030, there has been scant progress. At the same time demand for timber, which is expected to grow 37% by 2050, could rise even higher if more wood is used for construction – a climate solution to replace demand for high-carbon steel and cement.
Against this ​bleak backdrop, the most ambitious regulatory solution on offer is the EU’s deforestation regulation (EUDR), which will come into effect at the end of this year after twice being delayed. The question is, how much can it do to move the dial?
Under the regulation, importers bringing a range of commodities including wood and paper products onto the European market (or exporting ‌them from Europe) will have to prove they didn’t rely on recently deforested or degraded land. Operators and traders will have to provide the exact geo-coordinates of plots where commodities are sourced.
For the 141 countries classed as low risk, including the UK and all EU countries, there will be less stringent checks. These include Romania, home to much of Europe’s old growth and primary forests, where NGO’s have called out a swathe of illegalities.
Land that was classified as forest in 2020 can still be used for wood production, so long as it’s not converted into a plantation, for example. Since the EU relies on the Food and Agriculture Organization’s (FAO) definition of a forest as having at least 10% canopy cover, observers think enforcement could be challenging. By contrast, the U.N. Environment Programme definition is at least 30% canopy cover.
Jack Hurd, head of earth systems at the World Economic Forum, points out that encroachment on forests is often insidious. “It's very rare that earth-moving equipment rocks up to the edge ​of a natural forest, and the next thing you know, it's clear-cut. Usually, there is a selective harvesting regime going on that's quasi-legal, and they take a few more trees than they're supposed to, and then the big firms move out and sell the concession to somebody who's a little bit more risk-tolerant and, all of a sudden, the forest starts to get degraded, and ​then more people are settling in that area, then eventually it gets cleared.”
Leah Samberg is lead scientist at the Accountability Framework initiative, which advises companies on achieving and monitoring ethical supply chains. She says the difficulty of defining deforestation in the timber industry makes risk assessment, monitoring and verification critical.
The AFI’s latest ⁠analysis of CDP’s disclosure data shows the largest proportion of companies disclosing deforestation risk (43%) are in the timber sector. But just 11% of timber disclosures report that more than 90% of their sourcing is deforestation-free.
The EU has tried to cut deforestation in timber supply chains before, with the European Union Timber Regulation. But research by the Wyss Academy for Nature in Switzerland suggests that the EUTR substantially increased forest loss in ​the 52 most EU-trade dependent countries, between 2010 and 2019.
Supply chains were restructured so timber was diverted to less regulated markets and the conversion of forests to agriculture accelerated, with nothing to stop those agricultural commodities being exported to the EU, the researchers said.
With the EUDR, that door will be closed, but it can’t entirely prevent leakage, says the report’s author Stefano Jud. He points out that timber producers will be able to sell into ​China’s huge domestic market. “The Chinese only run into problems when they want to resell (after processing) to the EU.”
The EUDR’s requirement for full supply-chain traceability, is particularly challenging for the global wood pellet industry. But researchers in the U.S. anticipate that the trade will largely shift to unregulated Asian markets, with only a slight fall in global production.
“You need a global regime that avoids (these) kind of leakage effects (but) to be effective, you need to maintain those supply-chain relationships, because that's the way you can exert influence on the behaviour of producers.” That means building governance capacity in other countries, adds Jud.
Samberg has no doubt that the EU regulation is a “net positive for deforestation-free action globally, (thanks to) the awareness and resources it’s brought to the problem”. However, she adds, “the narrow focus on supply chain compliance, as opposed to broader transformation in sourcing areas, creates incentives to clean up your own supply chain (but) not solve the problem”.
It had been hoped EUDR would spur similar action in the markets where ​the EU sources the biggest volumes, and there is some evidence of progress.
The UK has said it will enact legislation consistent with the EUDR across the same range of deforestation-risk commodities; China, which had raised security concerns about geolocation data, may now be exploring pathways for cooperation with Europe.
And in Brazil, reports suggest that the country’s National Space Research Institute has developed technology to generate data at the granularity required by EUDR.
In ​Europe, meanwhile, the EUDR’s data requirement has spawned a host of companies to help importers trace timber origins. When Netherlands-based timber trader Timberhub set up its managed marketplace to purchase and supply timber, it set out to ensure it could trace every piece of timber on its platform to a verified and legal source. Now it also offers EUDR compliance as a service, which has brought new customers from the pulp and paper industries.
But co-founder Dimitris Pagkratis ‌says the penalties European importers ⁠will face for breaching the EUDR “will always be a rounding error next to the volume of trade. The real effect is the trade that quietly stops happening – illegal logging, and it is genuinely hard to size.”
Interpol gauges trade in illegally logged timber is worth between $51 billion and $152 billion annually, while Client Earth estimates 20% of it ends up in the EU. “We are regulating a flow that nobody currently measures well,” observes Pagkratis.
Subhra Bhattacharjee, director general of the Forest Stewardship Council, agrees that the EUDR is no cure-all. “Deforestation is a very complex problem, requiring measures coming at it from different angles with all kinds of actors involved – local, international, regional,” she says. “EUDR is addressing it from the demand side, at the same time, you need the supply side; the policing on the ground.”
Over 175 million hectares of forest is certified by the FSC, through over 1,700 forest management and 70,000 chain of custody certificates. But certification doesn’t mean compliance with the EUDR.
The FSC has been trying to build capacity to meet EUDR amongst its certificate holders by “turning it into a workable, applicable, practicable set of instructions for companies”, Bhattacharjee says.
While companies, investors and consumers rely on certification, there are numerous reports of wood being certified as FSC when it’s not. Last year, FSC members voted for a motion, tabled by ​NGOs and corporates, to assess what would be required to develop a global digital system for traceability ​and volume control within FSC-certified supply chains. A roadmap to implement the system by 2030 is ⁠due by the end of next year.
Some geolocation data is already being collected as part of a voluntary regulatory module for due diligence and risk assessments to meet EUDR.
One solution to deforestation risk promoted by the pulp and paper industry is to plant fast-growing hardwood species such as eucalyptus, particularly on the millions of hectares of land that have already been degraded by intensive cattle farming or agriculture. Read more
Environmental groups have long criticised large-scale eucalyptus plantations for their impacts on water resources, biodiversity and soils, though this is mainly where they replace natural forest ecosystems.
Brazil-based Suzano is the world’s largest pulp producer, and a big player in ​the paper and packaging industry. Its pulp is derived from eucalyptus plantations, occupying land that was once degraded pasture. The company stresses that it takes a broad watershed approach and selects its trees to suit different growing conditions. It’s had a zero-deforestation commitment since 2020, backed up by geolocation and traceability ​programmes.
Paulo Leime, managing director for Suzano’s operations in Europe, the Middle ⁠East and Africa, says that around Suzano’s 1.6 million hectares of plantations sit another 1.1m hectares of land that is being protected to allow it to regenerate.
Having natural forest around plantations allows better management of watersheds, and has brought valuable knowledge about which insects can be used instead of chemicals to combat pests.
“There is a business case for sustainability,” he says. “We plant a tree. It takes seven years to grow. We have to be looking to the next decades’ strategy to make sure we are taking care of the environment where we operate and the communities around that.”
Suzano is exploring a business model to finance restoration through the sale of carbon credits, in a venture with Rabobank, Santander, food company Marfrig and mining group Vale. Its first project, announced last year, aims to restore 1,200 hectares of Atlantic forest on land owned by another eucalyptus pulp producer, Veracel Celulose.
“Our biggest challenge with EUDR was ⁠how to build technology to ​make sure this information flowed according to the customers, because it's a very complex value chain,” says Leime. “If we include our operations, our customers’ operations, which will then sell to (others), how do you make sure this is traceable from the very beginning until the ​very end.”
Suzano’s answer has been to develop a proprietary system to demonstrate EUDR compliance, something that is bringing new business. Leime is looking forward to the regulation’s implementation: “It's going to level up the playing field.”
While monoculture plantation forests such as eucalyptus can be fragile in the face of drought and pests, Hurd at the World Economic Forum believes they “ultimately will win the day as the value of natural forest starts to get priced a little bit more in terms of its ecosystem services”.
Such forests offer a “better climate and ​environmental outcome than using the same land to grow a crop such as sugarcane”, he adds.
“Whether fast growing eucalyptus from a plantation on degraded land, longer rotation teak from a plantation established a hundred years ago, or the selective harvesting of topical hardwoods, the global demand for these products is, and will likely remain, strong,” he says.
“Society has to ask, and answer, the question: where do you want your wood to come from?”
